prompt: What is a landing zone?
hint: It is about every account, not one.

choices.text: The first account a company opens, configured with care
choices.why: One careful account is not the point. The point is that the next account is set up the same way.

choices.text: The multi-account set-up every new account starts from
choices.why: Right. Accounts, OUs, logging, guardrails and access, in place before the first workload arrives.

choices.text: The region a company chooses as its home
choices.why: Control Tower asks for a home region, but the landing zone is the whole arrangement, not a place.

choices.text: A VPC where new machines are first started
choices.why: The name sounds like a network. It is a set of accounts and the rules around them.

prompt: Match each part Control Tower creates to the shop's name for it.
hint: The third column of the table.

prompt: An engineer moves `shop-staging` from `Staging` to `Prod` with `aws organizations move-account`, in an organisation run by Control Tower. What follows?
hint: Who made the change, and who keeps the record of the tree?

choices.text: Control Tower refuses the move
choices.why: Organizations carries it out. Control Tower notices afterwards, which is what drift is.

choices.text: Nothing; Organizations and Control Tower are the same service
choices.why: Control Tower is built on Organizations and keeps its own picture of the tree; a change behind its back makes the two disagree.

choices.text: Control Tower reports drift, to be repaired from Control Tower
choices.why: Right. Once Control Tower runs the tree, changes go through it; a direct move is drift.

choices.text: The account is closed for leaving its OU
choices.why: Nothing closes an account for moving. It is reported, not punished.

prompt: What does Account Factory give a new account that `create-account` in Organizations does not?
hint: Lesson 2's question was about the next account.

choices.text: The landing zone's baseline
choices.why: Right. The trail reaches it, Config records, the OU's controls apply and the right people can sign in.

choices.text: A twelve-digit number of its own
choices.why: Every account has one, whichever way it was made.

choices.text: A default VPC in every region
choices.why: Every new account gets that from AWS, as lesson 2 showed in moto.

choices.text: Membership of the organisation
choices.why: `create-account` already makes a member; the difference is what arrives inside it.

prompt: A company has run eight accounts for two years without Control Tower and turns it on. How do the eight accounts get the landing zone's baseline?
hint: Account Factory makes new accounts; these exist.

choices.text: They have to be closed and created again through Account Factory
choices.why: Nothing has to be rebuilt. Existing accounts have their own way in.

choices.text: Their OUs are registered and the accounts enrolled
choices.why: Right. Enrolling applies the same baseline to an account that was made before, or invited.

choices.text: Automatically, the moment Control Tower is set up
choices.why: Control Tower governs what is registered with it. Accounts it does not know of stay as they are.

choices.text: They cannot: Control Tower needs a new organisation
choices.why: Control Tower can be set up on an existing organisation; most companies arrive with one.

prompt: Match each kind of control to what it is built from.
hint: The table's third column.

prompt: A detective control finds a bucket in `shop-prod` that the public can read. What happens to the bucket?
hint: Which kind of control refuses things?

choices.text: Config makes it private again
choices.why: A detective control undoes nothing. Remediation is a separate thing somebody has to set up.

choices.text: It is deleted at the next evaluation
choices.why: Nothing is deleted by a rule; that would be a worse incident than the one it found.

choices.text: Nothing; it is reported as non-compliant and somebody acts
choices.why: Right. Detective means after the fact: the finding appears in the Audit account, and a person fixes it.

choices.text: The account's SCPs are tightened so it cannot happen again
choices.why: No control changes another. A preventive control would have to be enabled on purpose.

prompt: The shop wants "every bucket must be encrypted" enforced, including buckets created before the rule. Which kind of control can see those old buckets?
hint: Two of the kinds act on a request or a template; one looks at what exists.

choices.text: Preventive, since an SCP applies to the whole account
choices.why: An SCP sees requests, not state. A bucket made last year makes no request today.

choices.text: Detective
choices.why: Right. A Config rule judges the recorded state of every resource, whenever it was made.

choices.text: Proactive, since it checks resources before they exist
choices.why: Before they exist is exactly why it cannot see the old ones.

choices.text: Any of the three, once it is mandatory
choices.why: Guidance says how much choice there is, not what a control can see.

prompt: Which controls are on in every landing zone and cannot be switched off?
hint: They protect the landing zone itself.

choices.text: The strongly recommended ones
choices.why: Those are AWS's advice; a company switches them on, and can leave them off.

choices.text: The mandatory ones
choices.why: Right. They guard the trail, the log bucket and the roles Control Tower made.

choices.text: The elective ones, once chosen
choices.why: Elective controls are for particular needs and are switched on and off OU by OU.

choices.text: Every detective control
choices.why: Kind and guidance are separate: a detective control may be mandatory, recommended or elective.

prompt: An account records 5,000 configuration items in a month at 0.003 dollars each. How many dollars is the recording?
hint: Items times the price.

prompt: Rule evaluations cost 0.001 dollars each for the first 100,000 of the month and 0.0008 for the next 400,000. How many dollars are 300,000 evaluations?
hint: Two tiers: the first 100,000, then the rest.

prompt: The organisation trail records every account's management events. A team adds its own trail in `shop-prod` for the same events. What does that cost?
hint: Which copy is free?

choices.text: Nothing, since management events are free
choices.why: Only the first copy is free. The organisation trail already is that copy.

choices.text: 0.000001 dollars per event, like data events
choices.why: That is the data events' line. A second copy of management events is the paid line.

choices.text: Nothing until the trail is moved to `log-archive`
choices.why: Where the records are delivered does not decide the price of recording them.

choices.text: 0.00002 dollars per event, 2 dollars per 100,000
choices.why: Right. The second copy is `SAE1-PaidEventsRecorded`, which `jq` read out of the offer file.

prompt: `aws controltower list-landing-zones` answered `500` in moto. What does that tell you?
hint: Whose error is it?

choices.text: moto has no Control Tower
choices.why: Right. moto implements none of the service, so nothing about Control Tower was run.

choices.text: The landing zone exists but is drifting
choices.why: Drift would be reported by Control Tower. There is no Control Tower to report it.

choices.text: Control Tower needs to be called in `us-east-1`
choices.why: The region is not the problem; moto fails the call wherever it is sent.

choices.text: The CLI version is too old for Control Tower
choices.why: The command exists in the CLI, which is why it reached moto at all.

prompt: Why does `landing-zone.sh` test the root's policy types before `enable-policy-type`?
hint: What is different about a new organisation in AWS?

choices.text: moto refuses to enable a type twice
choices.why: moto's root starts with none enabled. The test is for AWS.

choices.text: In AWS they are on already, and asking again fails
choices.why: Right. `PolicyTypeAlreadyEnabledException` plus `set -e` would end the run before a single OU exists.

choices.text: Enabling SCPs costs money, so it is done only once
choices.why: SCPs cost nothing at all. The reason is an error, not a price.

choices.text: Without it the guardrail would be attached to the wrong OU
choices.why: Which OU gets the guardrail is decided by the `--target-id`, not by this test.

prompt: In moto the wait loop in `account()` never sleeps. Why is it in the script at all?
hint: What did lesson 2 say AWS answers to `create-account`?

choices.text: To slow the script down so moto keeps up
choices.why: moto answers at once; nothing needs to keep up.

choices.text: Because `move-account` fails on an account less than ten seconds old
choices.why: No such rule exists. What fails is moving an account that does not exist yet.

choices.text: AWS answers `IN_PROGRESS` and builds the account in the background
choices.why: Right. Moving or using the account before it is `SUCCEEDED` would fail, so the script waits.

choices.text: To retry when the e-mail address is already taken
choices.why: A taken address is a `FAILED` state, and the loop stops the script on it rather than retrying.

prompt: Which of these did `landing-zone.sh` actually build in moto? Choose all that apply.
hint: The figure draws them solid.

choices.text: The OU `Security` with `log-archive` and `security` in it
choices.why: Right. `list-accounts-for-parent` showed both.

choices.text: The organisation trail delivering to `log-archive`
choices.why: No trail and no bucket were made; that needs a role in `log-archive` and CloudTrail.

choices.text: `security` as GuardDuty's delegated administrator
choices.why: Right. `list-delegated-administrators` named it.

choices.text: A Config recorder in every account
choices.why: Config is not in the script, so there are no detective controls either.

choices.text: The guardrail `protect-the-record` on `Security`
choices.why: Right, stored and attached; moto would not enforce it, as lesson 4 measured.

prompt: The shop's guardrail `protect-the-record` exempts `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`. What would break if it did not?
hint: Somebody has to write the bucket's policy once.

choices.text: Nothing, since SCPs do not apply to that role
choices.why: It is an ordinary role in a member account, so the SCPs above it apply.

choices.text: The management account could no longer sign in
choices.why: The guardrail denies a few S3 and CloudTrail actions, not taking the role on.

choices.text: GuardDuty would stop in `security`
choices.why: No GuardDuty action is in the guardrail; lesson 4's separate policy covers that.

choices.text: Nobody could put a bucket policy on the log bucket
choices.why: Right. `s3:PutBucketPolicy` would be denied to everyone in `Security`, the platform included, and CloudTrail could never be allowed to write there.

prompt: Order what has to exist before CloudTrail can deliver the organisation's records to `log-archive`.
hint: A bucket needs an account; a trail needs a bucket it may write to.
items: a bucket policy letting CloudTrail write
the organisation trail, created from the management account
trap: Creating the trail before the bucket policy is the usual slip: CloudTrail checks that it may write to the bucket when the trail is created.

prompt: A company with no compliance team, two engineers and Terraform everywhere asks which way to build its landing zone. Which answer fits it best?
hint: Weigh who will maintain it against what it must satisfy.

choices.text: Landing Zone Accelerator, for the largest baseline
choices.why: It is aimed at strict compliance requirements, which this company does not have, and it is a lot to run for two people.

choices.text: Control Tower with Account Factory for Terraform
choices.why: Right. AWS maintains the landing zone, and new accounts arrive as reviewed Terraform, which the team already works in.

choices.text: `landing-zone.sh` as it stands, run once
choices.why: It builds the shape and nothing inside the accounts, and a script run once fails the test of the next account.

choices.text: No landing zone until the company has more accounts
choices.why: The baseline is cheapest before the accounts multiply; afterwards it is a repair.

prompt: Which of these settles who may use the root user of `shop-prod`, something `landing-zone.sh` leaves undecided?
hint: Lesson 2 named it.

choices.text: An SCP denying everything to the root user
choices.why: An SCP can restrict a member's root user, but its credentials still exist; the management account can remove them instead.

choices.text: A detective control that reports root sign-ins
choices.why: It would tell somebody afterwards; the question is whether the credentials should exist at all.

choices.text: Removing member accounts' root credentials from the management account
choices.why: Right. IAM lets the management account remove them, so no password or key for `shop-prod`'s root exists to be stolen.

choices.text: Giving the root user's e-mail to the security team
choices.why: That decides who receives its mail, not who may sign in as it.
